entry.title: Do Chopped Carbon Fibers Actually Improve 3D-Printed Lattices? (We Tested It)

link.title: Do Chopped Carbon Fibers Actually Improve 3D-Printed Lattices? (We Tested It)

entry.content:
If you’ve spent any time reading about 3D printing and architected materials recently, you’ve probably seen the hype around Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) structures.

Because of their zero-mean-curvature geometry, structures like the Gyroid don’t have the sharp nodes or corners found in standard strut lattices. This lets them distribute stress evenly and absorb huge amounts of energy without collapsing prematurely.

Naturally, the next step engineers take to push performance further is to throw chopped carbon fibers into the filament. Higher stiffness, higher strength — problem solved, right?

Not quite.

In practice, the literature on chopped fiber TPMS lattices has been surprisingly mixed. In some tests, short carbon fibers make parts stiffer; in others, the added brittleness actually makes the printed lattice perform worse than its unreinforced polymer counterpart under heavy compression.

To figure out what’s actually going on, our team at NYU Abu Dhabi put together a systematic study looking at the intersection of material, density, and post-processing.

Here is what we found.

The Experiment: 5 Materials, 3 Densities, and Heat Treatment

We 3D-printed Gyroid lattices across relative densities ranging from 20% to 40% using five distinct material systems:

  • VeroWhite (PolyJet)
  • Nylon 12 (Selective Laser Sintering)
  • ABS (Fused Filament Fabrication / FFF)
  • PLA-CF (10% carbon fiber by volume)
  • PPA-CF (Polyphthalamide with 15% carbon fiber by volume)

We also took a subset of the PPA-CF lattices and subjected them to a post-print thermal annealing process (80°C for 8–12 hours) to see if heat-treating could unlock latent mechanical performance.

Key Takeaway 1: Reinforcement Needs Density

At low relative densities (20%), material choice barely made a difference. The architecture itself dominates the behavior, meaning thin walls flex and deform regardless of what they’re made of.

However, as relative density increased to 30% and 40%, the performance of the carbon fiber-reinforced PPA (PPA-CF) pulled ahead drastically. At 40% density, as-built PPA-CF gyroids achieved a peak stress outperforming PLA-CF by nearly 50%, sustaining load through a smooth, progressive strain-hardening regime.

Key Takeaway 2: Thermal Annealing is the Real Game-Changer

While adding chopped carbon fibers helps, post-print heat treatment is what truly elevates performance.

When we thermally annealed the PPA-CF gyroids, we saw:

  • Peak stress increase by ~40%
  • Toughness (energy absorption) jump by up to 60%
  • Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) values hitting 24–25 kJ/kg

To put that 24–25 kJ/kg number into perspective, it places these lightweight polymer-composite lattices into the performance envelope typically reserved for metallic TPMS structures (like titanium or steel lattices) — but at a fraction of the weight.

Key Takeaway 3: The Ductility Trade-Off

There is no free lunch in materials science.

While annealing significantly boosts peak load capacity and stiffness, it alters how the lattice fails. FEA simulations showed that fiber reinforcement increases localized stress concentration and plastic strain along load-bearing curves.

As a result, annealed PPA-CF lattices trade off some post-yield ductility. Instead of a perfectly flat, predictable crushing plateau, they experience minor stress drops corresponding to localized internal shear planes.

If your goal is absolute maximum strength and lightweight energy dissipation (think aerospace crash protection or defense applications), annealed PPA-CF is an exceptional choice. If you need a completely smooth, constant crushing force, unreinforced or untreated polymers might still have a role to play.

Final Thoughts

Architected metamaterials aren’t just about tweaking CAD geometry. The interplay between inner topology, fiber orientation, and thermal post-processing dictates how these parts actually behave in the real world.

By coordinating relative density with post-print annealing, chopped-fiber polymer lattices can bridge the gap between heavy metals and compliant plastics.

For the full deep dive, FEA models, and raw dataset, check out our paper published in Progress in Additive Manufacturing:

🔗 https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

Datasets: https://zenodo.org/records/18457274 and

Reference

Hussain, S., Mehraj, H., Moustafa, M. et al. Do chopped fibers matter? Process–structure–property relationships and thermal annealing effects in fiber-reinforced TPMS lattices.Prog Addit Manuf (2026). https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

entry.title: When Chopped Fibers Meet Gyroid Lattices: Unlocking Metallic-Level Energy Absorption in 3D Printed Polymers

link.title: When Chopped Fibers Meet Gyroid Lattices: Unlocking Metallic-Level Energy Absorption in 3D Printed Polymers

entry.content:
Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) lattices—particularly the gyroid architecture—have emerged as a transformative class of architected metamaterials. By decoupling structural performance from the intrinsic properties of the base material, they offer exceptional stiffness-to-weight ratios and progressive energy absorption.

But as we push the boundaries of additive manufacturing (AM), a critical question remains: How do we push polymeric TPMS lattices to perform closer to metallic structures without sacrificing their lightweight advantages?

In our recently published paper in Progress in Additive Manufacturing, my colleagues and I at NYU Abu Dhabi systematically investigated the process–structure–property relationships of fiber-reinforced TPMS lattices (Figure 1). Specifically, we looked at whether adding chopped carbon fibers, combined with post-print thermal annealing, could fundamentally alter the deformation mechanics of gyroid structures.

Here is a technical summary of what we found.

The Experimental Matrix

We didn't just look at one material. To isolate the effects of fiber reinforcement and architecture, we fabricated gyroid TPMS lattices across three relative densities (20%, 30%, and 40%) using five distinct polymeric systems:

  • VeroWhite (PolyJet)

  • Nylon 12 (SLS)

  • ABS (FFF)

  • PLA-CF (10% chopped carbon fiber, FFF)

  • PPA-CF (15% chopped carbon fiber, FFF)

We subjected these to quasi-static compression testing and validated the deformation mechanisms using non-linear Finite Element Analysis (FEA). We also applied a post-print thermal annealing process (80 °C for 8 hours) specifically to the PPA-CF specimens to unlock latent mechanical performance.

Key Discoveries: The Synergy of Density and Fibers

Our results showed that simply adding fibers to a low-density lattice isn't enough. The true magic happens at the intersection of high relative density and fiber reinforcement.

The 40% Density Threshold: At lower densities (20%), architectural compliance dominates, and material differences are less pronounced. However, at 40% relative density, the PPA-CF (CF15) lattices exhibited massive strain-hardening. The compressive stress increased from ~5 MPa at yield to over 15 MPa at a strain of 0.5, vastly outperforming neat polymers like ABS and Nylon 12, which suffered from premature collapse or stress plateaus.

Progressive Collapse: Unlike more brittle composites (like PLA-CF) or compliant resins (VeroWhite), the as-built PPA-CF gyroids exhibited extended plateau regions. The chopped fibers promoted effective stress redistribution, leading to a progressive, layer-by-layer collapse ideal for energy absorption.

The Game Changer: Thermal Annealing

The most significant breakthrough of our study was the effect of thermal post-processing on the PPA-CF lattices. Annealing at 80 °C fundamentally modified the post-yield behavior:

  • Peak Stress: Increased by ~40%.

  • Toughness (Energy Absorption): Increased by up to 60%.

Why does this happen? Annealing increases crystallinity in the PPA matrix, relaxes residual stresses from the FFF process, and drastically improves the fiber–matrix interfacial bonding.

Approaching Metallic Performance

To put these numbers into perspective, we calculated the Specific Energy Absorption (SEA).

Annealed PPA-CF gyroids achieved an SEA of 24–25 kJ/kg at densities of just 200–430 kg/m³.

To contextualize this: these values are highly competitive with single-phase aluminum and titanium alloy TPMS structures, and they achieve similar energy absorption to steel-based metamaterials at a density reduction of nearly 1,500 kg/m³ (Figure 2). We effectively bridged the performance gap between lightweight polymeric foams and heavy metallic lattices.

The Engineering Trade-Off: Strength vs. Ductility

As materials engineers know, there is no free lunch. While thermal annealing unlocked massive gains in peak strength and toughness, it introduced a critical trade-off.

Our FEA and experimental data showed that annealing reduces the post-elastic ductility of the base composite. Instead of a smooth, continuous plateau, the annealed lattices (particularly at 30% density) exhibited localized stress drops and inner shear plane failures. The fibers, while highly aligned in the extrusion direction to resist in-plane membrane stresses, are poorly oriented to resist out-of-plane shear stresses once significant plasticization occurs.

The takeaway for design: If your application requires a perfectly smooth, constant plateau stress, as-built PPA-CF or ductile neat polymers might be preferable. But if your design criteria prioritize maximum peak load-bearing capacity and total energy absorption per unit weight, annealed PPA-CF is the superior choice.

Conclusion

Our study demonstrates that material selection is just as critical as geometric design in architected metamaterials. By coordinating the control of relative density, chopped carbon fiber reinforcement, and thermal post-processing, we can engineer polymer-based TPMS lattices that rival metallic structures in energy absorption, while maintaining a fraction of the weight.

This opens up exciting new avenues for lightweight impact protection, aerospace structural components, and biomedical implants.

📖 Read the full open-access paper here: https://doi.org/10.1007/s40964-026-01791-9

Data and supplementary materials are available on Zenodo.

What are your thoughts on the trade-offs of thermal annealing in FFF composites? Have you experimented with post-processing TPMS structures for specific energy absorption? Let me know in the comments or connect with me on Website/Bluesky/Lens.

entry.summary: By combining chopped carbon fiber reinforcement with thermal post-processing, 3D-printed polymer gyroids can achieve metallic-level energy absorption at a fraction of the weight of aluminum or titanium.
